items.title: Ed Garland Interview, 1958-08-08; 1958-09-03
items.q: the man who learned me how to play a four-string bass was Andrew Kimball. Oh, yeah. Henry Kimball.

ctx.x: And when I learned how to finger E string, I was, the man who learned me how to play a four-string bass was Andrew Kimball. Oh, yeah. Henry Kimball. Henry Kimball. Henry Kimball. Henry Kimball, Robichaud's bass player. And you may believe it or not, I was the oldest one who could go sit in Robichaud's band and play. Robichaud didn't allow that, you know, those certain days, them guys, you know.
No, no, I guess it wasn't allowed.

items.title: 68090_Ed Garland oral history interview
items.q: So he says to me, 'Eddie, I'm going to tell you what I want you to do. You get that E string and you put that E-string back on the bass and play it, and I'm going to show you how to finger it.'

ctx.x: Then when I really want to get to bowing, I went to St. Catherine's Hall, where Henry Kimball was playing.

items.title: Ed Garland Interview, 1971-04-20
items.q: He made me put that string on that bass and he showed me how to finger.

ctx.x: Well, as far as I know, they always have fourth strings. They always have? Up to mine. But I used to, most of the boys used to take the E string off. Uh huh. Because the finger though, fourth string, most of the, I was playing, I was playing fourth strings, was, I was playing in the theater and the symphony band. Uh huh. Just like Bowen. They bowed. Yeah. And I was in theater. But the man, because of me playing, using the fourth string, Hendrick Kimball. Oh yeah.
